Seven Hillview Terrace factories up for tender at $51.6 mil; four more on sale for $33.6 mil
article:
A portfolio of seven terraced factory properties in Hillview Terrace within Bukit Batok have been launched for sale by public tender.

The adjoining 999-year leasehold properties — located at 36A, 36B, 38, 38A, 38B, 38C and 38D Hillview Terrace — have a guide price of $51.6 million, said Colliers in an Oct 27 release.

The plots span a combined site area of 31,199 sq ft, which means the price works out to about $1,655 psf on the land area.

While the plots are zoned for residential use under the URA Master Plan, they have been approved for general industrial use. They have a gross plot ratio of 1.62.

Buyers may acquire the site for continued industrial or warehousing use. As privately held factories, they are not subject to JTC approval.

Alternatively, the site’s underlying residential zoning allows developers the option to explore redevelopment.

Subject to approval, an additional 0.30 plot ratio may be granted for the site for residential redevelopment. This would raise the maximum allowable plot ratio to 1.92, Colliers added.

“The flexibility to retain the existing industrial use or explore future redevelopment should appeal to a broad range of owner-occupiers, investors and developers,” said Steven Tan, executive director for capital markets and investment services at Colliers.

The tender for the portfolio will close at 3pm on Dec 1.

Separately, Colliers is also marketing another group of properties in the area. Comprising four freehold semi-detached factories at 31, 33, 35 and 35 Annex Hillview Terrace, the portfolio is up for sale by private treaty with a $33.63 million asking price.

The four properties occupy 19,781 sq ft of residential land with a gross plot ratio of 1.62. Similar to the properties up for sale by tender, the site could potentially qualify for an additional 0.30 if redeveloped for residential use.

Together, the two portfolios represent around 50,980 sq ft of land.

The availability of the freehold portfolio gives buyers “another option to consider alongside the tender site”, said Tan. “For developers, the combination of contiguous land, residential zoning, and long leasehold and freehold tenures creates an opportunity that is difficult to replicate in the area.”

The latest industrial transaction in Hillview Terrace was the sale of a 999-year factory with a land area of 5,672 sq ft that fetched $8.5 million, or $1,499 psf.

Before that, two 999-year factories changed hands in April: One occupied a 6,836 sq ft site that fetched $9.3 million ($1,360 psf), and another, a 4,150 sq ft site that was sold for $5.8 million ($1,398 psf).

title: Nvidia vs AMD: Which Chip Stock Is the Better Buy Today?
article:
Nvidia
(NASDAQ: NVDA) and
AMD
(NASDAQ: AMD) are two of the leading players in the market for advanced AI chips.
Yet, their business models, profitability and valuations differ.
Nvidia is the more established – and far larger – company.
As of 16 October 2026, it had a market capitalisation of US$5.2 trillion, compared to AMD’s US$863 billion.
But there are benefits to being a challenger, and both companies have been swept up in the enthusiasm for
all things AI
.
Nvidia: The Dominant Player
Nvidia is the undisputed market leader in graphics processing units (GPUs), each of which can have many cores that allow for processing of complex operations simultaneously, making them suitable for training the large language models (LLMs) that are the foundation of generative AI.
Notably, Nvidia also owns the CUDA computing platform, which allows developers to use GPUs for general-purpose processing, and not just the graphics rendering they were traditionally designed for.
Many developers in AI have been trained to use CUDA, which only works with Nvidia chips, creating a barrier to entry for other chip companies.
Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary of the
AI boom
– its revenue rose by 3.5x to US$216 billion in its financial year ending January 2026 (FY2026), compared to FY2024.
Its margins are equally impressive, with a gross margin of 71% in FY2026. The company also generated nearly US$103 billion in cash from operating activities in the same year.
Part of this windfall has gone into investments and partnerships with key players in the AI ecosystem, from frontier labs OpenAI and Anthropic, to AI data centre operators such as
CoreWeave
(NASDAQ: CRWV).
Some market participants have likened these arrangements to circular financing, since all are important Nvidia customers.
Related articles:
Amazon and 2 Other Winners: 3 Growth Stocks to Buy Now and Hold for the Long Term
More Than Just Chips: Why the AI Revolution Needs These 5 Companies
AMD: The Upstart
AMD’s traditional strength was in making central processing unit (CPU) chips, which were initially overlooked when the AI boom first started.
However, the increasing focus on inference and AI agents means that demand for CPUs is expected to increase by 10x from 2025 to 2030.
Indeed, Muse. from
Meta Platforms
’ (NASDAQ: META), and OpenAI’s Dots, the two companies’ respective AI agents, both run on AMD’s EPYC-branded CPUs.
AMD is also challenging Nvidia in the GPU space with its Instinct product, which it is combining with its CPUs, networking, and ROCm software stack to create Helios, its fully integrated AI infrastructure offering.
Unlike CUDA, AMD’s ROCm is open-source and can run on GPUs from other manufacturers, even Nvidia’s.
If ROCm is able to attract more developers and users, it may even be able to breach the CUDA moat.
Hyperscalers from Meta to
Microsoft
(NASDAQ: MSFT) are spending huge sums of money on AI chips and looking for alternatives to Nvidia so it doesn’t exercise excessive market power.
This presents AMD with an opportunity to take market share from the leader.
Related articles:
3 US Stocks That Doubled in a Year: Should You Buy, Hold or Take Profits?
5 AI-Related Growth Stocks to Supercharge Your Investment Portfolio
Which Chipmaker Has the Stronger Business?
For now, Nvidia is still far ahead of AMD, which had US$35 billion in revenue for its financial year ending December 2025 (FY2025), 1.5x its FY2023 revenue.
But this was still just 16% of Nvidia’s top line for the comparable period.
Both have data centre businesses that are growing strongly.
In Nvidia’s most recent quarter, 2QFY2027, its data centre revenue grew by 2.2x to US$89 billion on strong demand for its cutting-edge Blackwell chips.
AMD’s data centre business experienced similar levels of year-on-year growth, with the segment’s revenue of US$6.7 billion being 2.1x the year-ago figure.
Yet, Nvidia’s business is far more profitable, a reflection of its market leadership.
For example, its 1HFY2027 net income margin was 66%, compared with AMD’s 17% for 1HFY2026.
Despite its market leadership, Nvidia isn’t resting on its laurels.
Earlier this year, it announced the Vera CPU, purpose-built for agentic AI, which it claims is twice as efficient as, and 50% faster than traditional CPUs.
Still, the desire from hyperscalers to see a viable alternative supplier to Nvidia should ensure that AMD gets its share of AI-driven demand.
AMD also stands to benefit from operating leverage, as fixed costs are spread across a larger business.
Its gross profit margin rose from 40% in 2QFY2025 to 54% in 2QFY2026, and is expected to reach 56% in 3QFY2026.
Looking ahead, both businesses must continue to innovate to stay ahead of the competition.
Size also gives Nvidia the advantage here.
In 1HFY2027, it spent US$13.4 billion on R&D, nearly 3x the US$4.9 billion AMD spent in its equivalent period.
It’s also worth noting that Nvidia’s R&D expenditure was just 7.5% of revenue over that period, compared to 22.6% for AMD.
Valuation and Risk
Given Nvidia’s superior economics, one might expect it to attract a premium valuation to AMD.
However, this is not the case.
Nvidia’s forward price-to-earnings ( P/E) ratio is 24.9x, while its PEG ratio (which accounts for expected earnings growth) is 0.5x.
The equivalent figures for AMD are 39.5x and 0.6x respectively.
Part of the explanation for this paradox is that AMD has already seen a significant run-up in its share price – it is 137% higher in the year to 16 October 2026.
Nvidia’s share price, in contrast, rose by just 13% over the same period.
Although both companies face similar risks, including the bursting of the AI bubble and the cyclicality of the
semiconductor industry
reasserting itself, AMD’s higher valuation also means that it is more susceptible to changes in investor sentiment.
Nvidia, meanwhile, might be doubly exposed to the underperformance of the companies in the AI ecosystem it has invested in.
In the past week, for example, CoreWeave’s share price has fallen by 24% as investors fret over its debt levels and ability to scale its business.
Get Smart: Which AI Chip Stock Would I Buy?
Nvidia and AMD offer two distinct ways to invest in the growth of AI computing.
Nvidia benefits from its established leadership, strong software ecosystem and proven profitability.
AMD offers the potential for significant growth and operating leverage if it successfully expands its market share.
However, given its superior economics and lower valuation, Nvidia might be the pick between the two, despite understandable scepticism about how much more a US$5.2 trillion company can grow.

title: Woodside sells stake in long-stalled Timor-Leste LNG project
article:
(Oct 27): Woodside Energy Group Ltd has sold its operating interest in the long-stalled Greater Sunrise liquefied natural gas (LNG) project to a Timor-Leste state-owned company.

The sale of the 33.44% stake is worth as much as US$200 million, Woodside said Tuesday in a statement, although most of that is dependent on the project being built. The small nation has long pushed for the development of the two fields that make up Greater Sunrise and a LNG plant in a bid to tap potentially billions of dollars of revenue.

Timor Gap will now control the entire project, after last month agreeing to buy out a third shareholder, Osaka Gas Corp. An independent assessment from 2018 estimated the development cost at US$15.6 billion.

For years Woodside and the Timorese government have argued over whether to build the liquefaction plant locally or pipe the gas to Australia. The fields have contingent resources of 5.1 trillion cubic feet of gas and 226 million barrels of condensate, according to Timor Gap.

title: Alibaba wins challenge to Pentagon’s Chinese army blacklisting
article:
(Oct 27): Alibaba Group Holding Ltd won a US court ruling in its challenge to a Department of Defense blacklist that identifies the e-commerce leader as a supporter of the Chinese military.

A federal judge in San Jose, California, on Monday ordered the Trump administration to stop enforcing a ban on the Pentagon doing business with any company that engages in “lobbying activities” for Hangzhou, China-based Alibaba.

title: This oil tanker tycoon's WhatsApp messages drive big market moves
article:
LONDON/SINGAPORE (Oct 27): The messages from the world’s biggest supertanker owner often begin with pleasantries: “Dear Ladies and Gentlemen.”

Within minutes, the WhatsApps are the talk of the oil-tanker industry, a multibillion-dollar corner of the energy market that’s been plunged into chaos by the Iran war this year, and where word of mouth is the main way information spreads. The details vary, but the messages to shipbrokers from Sinokor Group, the South Korean company controlled by tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung, mostly boil down to the same thing — one of its vessels has just been hired at a new sky-high rate to ferry oil out of the Persian Gulf.

Some messages detail a new contract, listing the ship, counterparty and eyewatering price. Others just refer loosely to negotiations underway. The format fluctuates from terse strings of numbers and names to full sentences and florid signoffs: “Very respectfully. Thank you very much and best regards,” concludes one message sent to brokers in August, and seen by Bloomberg. Usually, in the days that follow, the global benchmark price set by London’s Baltic Exchange takes another leap higher.

What would simply be fodder for gossip in most industries, brokers say that Sinokor’s WhatsApp messages have for months played an outsized role in setting the cost of transporting oil around the world. Rates for very-large crude carriers (VLCC) — the biggest kind of oil tanker — have soared more than 1,600% this year amid disruptions caused by the war, creating an unprecedented boom for the industry, but throwing a spotlight on the arcane system used to price the world’s shipping contracts, and the centuries-old institution that manages it.

The world of oil tanker rates is coming under fresh scrutiny this week, as hearings begin in a London lawsuit brought against the Baltic Exchange by trader Mercuria Energy Group, which argues that the benchmark rate is no longer fit for purpose because of the disruptions caused by the Iran war. Mercuria has complained to the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority about the benchmark, according to its legal filings, and at least one other market participant has also contacted the regulator, according to a person with knowledge of the complaint, who asked not to be identified because it is not public.

See also: Maersk owner seeks investments in Asia startups with new office

The Mercuria case doesn’t refer to Sinokor or its role in the market. Mercuria argues that a near-cessation of normal commercial shipments through the Strait of Hormuz since the war began meant that there was no basis on which to calculate the oil tanker market’s most important reference price, known as TD3C, which measures the cost of shipping oil from inside the Persian Gulf to China.

But the war is also shining a light on wider questions about how the benchmark is determined, especially as Sinokor’s dominance of the market has expanded. Every day, a select number of shipbrokers submit assessments of the market to the Baltic Exchange, which uses them to publish a price for the TD3C index.

While Middle Eastern state producers are having growing success in moving their oil out of the gulf, the trade is still largely covert by nature, reducing the flow of verifiable data.

See also: Rhine drops below shipping threshold as freight costs rise

The result, shipowners, traders and brokers say, is that Sinokor’s swaggering WhatsApps are often a key source of information available for assessing the Persian Gulf tanker market, and therefore for setting the global cost of shipping oil.

Sinokor has “a huge influence on the market dynamics and the fundamentals of what’s happening on the VLCC market”, said Joel Grau, chief executive officer at shipping insurer Zostera Marine and a professor at the National Maritime College of Ireland.

To be sure, the tanker market is being supported by a genuine supply squeeze, with more vessels tied up on longer and unusual routes or waiting to collect oil outside the gulf, and as Iran escalates missile and drone strikes on ships.

But nearly two decades after uproar over the Libor rate of borrowing, the scrutiny of the Baltic Exchange's main tanker rate is once again raising questions over the reliability of a financial benchmark that prices billions of dollars in derivatives and is set not by trades but by the assessments of market participants.

“I will of course still carry out my duties, but have we (the Baltic) taken any legal advice on the questionable market situation,” Christopher Loveday, an assessor for TD3C at the Baltic Exchange, asked a colleague in mid-March, according to a Mercuria legal filing. He expressed concern that the Baltic could face “issues” with market participants “like the Libor situation a decade or so ago”, according to the filing. (There’s no suggestion in Mercuria’s legal filings that the wrongdoing that led to the Libor scandal is at play at the Baltic Exchange, nor has any regulator or other party suggested as such.)

The importance of TD3C itself is already being eroded. Open interest on the underlying derivatives contracts has declined, and industry insiders say they’re increasingly focused on a new Baltic index called TD34 that prices the cost of shipping oil from just outside of the Strait of Hormuz to Asia.

This story is based on interviews with over a dozen people involved in oil tanker markets, most of whom asked not to be identified discussing private interactions and business dealings.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Sinokor didn’t respond to requests for comment. The Baltic Exchange and Mercuria declined to comment. The FCA said it can’t comment on engagement with individual firms and that it has been monitoring the impact of the Iran war since the conflict began.

In its defence, the Baltic Exchange, which is owned by Singapore Exchange Ltd, has said that its decision to keep publishing TD3C wasn’t taken lightly. Mercuria is asking the court to retroactively suspend the index. However, the Baltic’s lawyers said that doing so would mean dissolving more than eight months of pricing and that “such a claim is without precedent in this jurisdiction or, to the Baltic’s knowledge, in any other”.

It was barely two weeks into the Iran war, on March 12, when brokers received a notification from Sinokor that it had hired out a ship to sail from the United Arab Emirates port of Zirku to Asia at a rate of at least 700 Worldscale points — far above the Baltic’s assessment for that day of 348.89. The Worldscale system is a standardised way of comparing tanker freight rates across different routes.

At the time, prices had already been soaring for months after Sinokor, until then a relatively smaller player, suddenly embarked on a massive supertanker buying spree with backing from container shipping giant MSC Mediterreanean Shipping Co.

The aggressive move gave Chung — the deeply private scion of a Korean shipping family — a level of influence in the tanker market that insiders say is unprecedented, and meant that Sinokor was positioned to reap huge profits when the war started.

By the time of Sinokor’s March WhatsApp, the Baltic Exchange was facing turmoil of its own, as shipbrokers grappled with how to calculate the cost of shipping from a Saudi Arabian port that was effectively inaccessible due to the war. Some began using a still-functioning Saudi port on the Red Sea for their TD3C assessments, but the exchange intervened and insisted that the benchmark price must continue to reflect loadings from inside the Persian Gulf.

By March 16, the Baltic’s rate jumped to almost 600 Worldscale points, equivalent to US$602,000 ($771,162) a day, as traders struggled to assess a trade that appeared to have stalled, and with barely any visibility of deals being done other than Sinokor’s notice.

Prices continued to swing wildly in the coming weeks, and in late April Mercuria filed a lawsuit alleging that it had suffered losses in the hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of distortions in the benchmark, though its lawyers said in May that it was not looking to “extract money from an exchange”. The company since removed the figure from its claim.

Mercuria argues that the index should be suspended immediately, and that since the Iran war began the route no longer serves its intended function. For its part, the Baltic’s argues that would be an unprecedented move and that if that request were granted there would be “chaotic market-wide consequences”, including for the multibillion-dollar derivatives market linked to TD3C.

For decades, the Baltic Exchange’s Middle East to Asia benchmark has stood at the heart of the oil tanker market, used as a reference point in long-term contracts for supertanker deals — including for vessels sailing elsewhere in the world — and underpinning a large derivatives market. The original TD3 route measured the cost of travelling to Japan, but was replaced about a decade ago with TD3C, to reflect China’s growing dominance as an oil importer.

The rate is published just after 4pm London time every day, based on the average of assessments provided by nine brokers. The individual brokers submit their estimates shortly before the price is issued, although the Baltic Exchange can occasionally ask for justification for the figures, one of the people said.

Mercuria’s lawsuit alleged that TD3C was being distorted, and its lawyers argued that the handful of ships transiting Hormuz in the early months of the war should not qualify as fixtures for setting the benchmark rate.

By the summer, however, the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf was becoming a steady stream, as producers and traders settled into a new “dark shuttle” system — using dedicated tankers making return journeys under cover of night before offloading oil onto ships waiting empty just outside the gulf.

Bloomberg reported in early July that Sinokor had emerged as a major owner of supertankers moving crude through the strait of Hormuz. But the level of information about ships and cargoes operating in the region for the most part remained extremely limited.

It was around that time that the Sinokor messages — referred to among industry insiders as “blasts” — began to accelerate. Sinokor owner Chung already had a reputation in shipping circles for creating sprawling WhatsApp groups with representatives from individual brokerage firms or counterparties, usually including large numbers of Sinokor employees as well.

In late July, when TD3C had begun to retreat following the interim peace deal between the US and Iran that notionally lowered the risk of attack in Hormuz, Sinokor “blasted” out that it had hired out a ship at 465 Worldscale points, about 60 points higher than where the market was assessed that day. The difference is the equivalent to just over US$60,000 a day in earnings.

Sinokor sent out at least five missives in August, each announcing progressively higher rates. By Aug 21, the company told the market that it hired a ship out at 1,350 Worldscale points, almost three times the level of just under a month earlier.

In the months to come, the market went parabolic, surging from around 400 points in late July, to almost 1,320 points in October. Supertankers in the Persian Gulf — and any deals still tied to TD3C— were now earning more than US$1.4 million a day.

The potential payoff for Sinokor and its partner MSC is huge. Sinokor is listed as the manager of 83 supertankers on the Equasis maritime database, many of which are operating in or around the Middle East. Most industry figures see the company controlling more vessels than that in reality when charter deals are added in too.

Using a gauge of average supertanker earnings across the world, a fleet of 83 ships would have pulled in on average of about US$143 million a month last year. That jumped to US$509 million by July this year, US$1.4 billion in September, and US$2.1 billion in October, based on the average for the month so far. In reality, it depends where the vessels are sailing, and those figures don't account for costs and days where ships aren't hired. (Some of the company’s ships have been hit in Hormuz recently, potentially reducing the number of days its tankers can earn money while they undergo repairs.) By comparison, Sinokor’s revenue for the whole of 2025, which also includes a container shipping arm, was US$5.5 billion, according to accounts published in South Korea.

While the financial rewards for companies like Sinokor willing to take the risk of crossing Hormuz are significant, the journeys also ultimately provided a vital lifeline to global energy markets. Worst case-scenario forecasts of US$200 a barrel crude oil prices never materialised, partly as a result of the ships that continued to cross Hormuz. Sinokor itself carried an estimated 37% of the oil that passed through the Strait of Hormuz last month, Bloomberg reported last week.

For many in the industry, the crucial question is how literally to take the Sinokor messages, which have become less frequent since the summer.

Several people involved in tanker markets said Sinokor's WhatsApps can leave room for interpretation around parts of the rate being publicised, like who pays for insurance, or the ship’s destination.

And the already opaque shipping market has become even harder to track as a result of the Iran war, as most ships in the Middle East have stopped broadcasting satellite signals that make their movements easy to follow.

Tracking and satellite images show that while some of the bookings the company broadcast went exactly as advertised, others are less clear. At least one ship that Sinokor said would sail from the Middle East to Asia in early August hasn’t left the Indian Ocean and Persian Gulf since then.

To be sure, charterers and shipowners will sometimes privately agree to change the route they’re due to sail, while bookings can also fall through.

The Baltic Exchange’s policies say that panellists should use discretion over the relative value they attribute to data they gather and — in cases where there is little or no activity on a route for a period of time — must apply their “expert judgement of the wider market” to provide an assessment.

Of 130 published days between early March and early September, the Baltic Exchange said in its defence that there were 12 instances where one broker didn’t provide the Baltic with an assessment for the route, citing difficulties in assessing the market. Last month, a different broker said that it would no longer input data for the route on an indefinite, but temporary basis, the exchange added in its defence for the court case.

“There is an element of trust when you are determining the price of shipping oil,” said Halvor Ellefsen, a London-based director at Fearnleys Shipbrokers UK Ltd. “With such a dominant player making bullish uncorroborated proclamations, although lacking underlying contractual details, it has never been more difficult to figure out where in reality TD3C sits. TD34 has by and large taken over from TD3C as a reliable benchmark."

title: Japan vows to address cyber attack on FX with urgency
article:
(Oct 27): Japan will address the damage stemming from a cyber attack on a foreign exchange trading platform with a sense of urgency but no new attacks have been detected, the nation’s finance minister said.

“Given how rapidly these incidents and circumstances evolve, we will continue to call on financial authorities to respond appropriately and swiftly as developments unfold,” Satsuki Katayama told reporters on Tuesday.

“There’s a sense of crisis shared globally” with regards to cybersecurity, she added, citing discussions with her Group of Seven counterparts in Bangkok last week.

Katayama spoke after dozens of businesses in Japan reported breaches to their systems and potential leaks of client data in recent weeks — at a time when concerns are mounting around the world about the use of artificial intelligence to take advantage of cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

In one of the latest incidents, IT services provider GMO Internet Group reported unauthorised access to its foreign-exchange trading platform, with some customers flagging transactions they hadn’t initiated.

Katayama said five FX firms had reported customers affected by the GMO incident, adding that she had received no reports of new unauthorised transactions.

See also: Chinese carmakers overtake Japan in Europe for first time

GMO sought government assistance on Saturday to help disrupt the source of the attacks. Chief executive officer Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post that the company had received a ransom demand for US$50 million in cryptocurrency, which it refused to pay.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi instructed her cabinet on Monday to draw up emergency measures by the end of next week in response to a wave of cyberattacks targeting Japanese companies.

At a regular press conference on Tuesday, Economy Minister Ryosei Akazawa said the government would offer smaller companies free consultation services on boosting their cybersecurity.

Cyberattacks and the discovery of vulnerabilities in PHP programming language used in some websites have made a swift response an urgent priority for businesses and the government. Several political parties called for stronger measures last week.

In recommendations submitted to Takaichi on Oct 23, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) said the recent wave of cyberattacks constituted a serious crisis that could be described as “the eve of a cyber emergency,” threatening Japan’s national security. It warned that “AI cyber saturation attacks,” in which artificial intelligence automatically identifies system vulnerabilities and launches attacks simultaneously, could occur in the near future.

The party also proposed creating a response headquarters led by the prime minister’s office, while accelerating efforts to improve the capabilities of the Self-Defense Forces and police and strengthen cooperation with allies. In the financial sector, it called for the public and private sectors to work together to steadily implement defensive measures.

Masaaki Taira, a former digital minister who led the drafting of the recommendations, said attackers are using AI to mount attacks faster and on a broader scale than before, while companies are still relying on people to defend themselves. “Structurally, it has become AI versus humans,” he said. The government needs to work with leading AI companies to build a system capable of using AI for defense, he added.

One concern common is securing specialist personnel. With highly skilled private-sector cybersecurity professionals such as white-hat hackers in mind, the LDP called for the creation of a new personnel and compensation system that would “break through the rigidities of the civil-service system and enable compensation commensurate with market value.”

Behind these proposals is a recognition that government salaries are insufficient compared with those in the private sector. According to the National Personnel Authority, the government can offer annual compensation of as much as ¥33.8 million under its fixed-term appointment system to private-sector personnel with specialised expertise. The latest data show 490 people are employed under the system, but none is receiving compensation at the highest level on a monthly-pay basis.

“Annual compensation of ¥33.8 million is by no means low, but there are limits to how far that level of pay can attract people who are already highly valued in the private sector,” said Sumio Morita, senior managing director at human-resources consultancy Towers Watson.

title: Microsoft to offer buyouts to 60,000 workers in new cost cut
article:
(Oct 27): Microsoft Corp will offer buyouts to about 60,000 workers, representing roughly a quarter of its total staff, as part of the company’s efforts to trim costs and retool its workforce for the artificial intelligence (AI) era.

Some personnel in the US, Canada, India and the UK at a vice-president level and below will be eligible, said a Microsoft spokesperson.

Divisions such as Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance are fully participating in the offer, according to people familiar with the terms. Certain pools of employees, including some focused on data centres, sales, marketing, cybersecurity and quantum computing, aren’t eligible, the people said. Microsoft declined to comment on these specifics.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” chief people officer Amy Coleman said in a note to staff Monday. Workers will receive benefits similar to a standard severance package, the spokesperson said.

The world’s largest software maker has shed tens of thousands of workers in waves of lay-offs in recent years. In July, it offered buyouts to retirement-age employees, and more than 30% of the roughly 8,750 eligible people took the offer. Microsoft expects far fewer personnel to accept the latest buyout proposal compared with the voluntary retirement programme, the spokesperson said.

See also: Apple debuts US$699 water-resistant iPad mini with OLED screen

Microsoft’s headcount as of the end of June was 223,000. The figure has been largely flat since 2022, about the time Microsoft began spending heavily on AI and data centres — squeezing budgets and hiring elsewhere in the company.

The company is scheduled to report financial results on Wednesday, and investors will be laser-focused on signs that the heavy spending on AI is paying off. Microsoft shares rose about 1% at midday in New York.

Other companies have sought to shrink headcount as they redirect spending to AI infrastructure. Google offered voluntary buyouts in a number of units last year, CNBC reported. Meta Platforms Inc’s headcount is down by more than 20,000 from a late 2022 peak. Both are among the biggest spenders on data centre infrastructure.

See also: Apple's iPhone Duo hits stores in face of short supply, high demand

The Microsoft spokesperson said the company wants employees who are engaged on the hard problems it’s trying to solve. That echoes other tech bosses, who’ve publicly made clear that continued employment means embracing a faster pace of work and change.

Elon Musk in 2022 famously gave Twitter employees the choice to be “extremely hardcore”, or take a severance payment. Earlier this year, Business Insider reported that a Google executive told employees in his organisation that those who weren’t “all in” on AI could have a voluntary buyout package.

Workers deciding whether to take a buyout typically assess their savings and whether they’re at risk of lay-offs later. Midcareer professionals also consider the job market and how long it might take them to find a new role, or whether the package gives them enough runway to make a pivot. Buyouts typically go to more senior, higher-cost staff, as with Microsoft’s round of early retirement offers, and offer more generous terms than a lay-off.

In some cases, Microsoft will try to retain top talent if employees opt to take the buyout offer, the spokesperson said.

The buyouts give Microsoft units “another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs”, Coleman wrote in the memo.

title: Iran war boosts Malaysian data centre appeal, SD Guthrie says
article:
(Oct 27): Malaysia is expected to attract more interest as a data centre hub following the outbreak of the US-Iran war, according to SD Guthrie Bhd (KL:SDG), giving the palm oil giant and the country’s biggest landowner an opportunity to capitalise on the boom.

Even before the Middle East conflict, Malaysia was already drawing data centre investment from companies including Alphabet Inc’s Google, Amazon.com Inc and Microsoft Corp. Over the weekend, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said Masayoshi Son of SoftBank Group Corp chose locations in the country for US$50 billion in technology investments.

While the war wasn’t cited as a factor in Son’s investment, SD Guthrie president and group chief executive officer Mohd Haris Mohd Arshad said Malaysia was the “most stable country” in Southeast Asia for building data centres. The world’s biggest palm oil planter by acreage previously flagged plans to use some of its lower-yielding land for industrial development to tap into the data centre boom.

The Middle East had been particularly attractive for data centre investment because of its abundant energy options, but the war has heightened risks in the region, Haris said during an interview on Friday, his first with foreign media since taking the helm in January.

“If you’re going to build data centres for US$10 billion, you’re not going to put it in a place where you might be bombed,” he said. “We are riding that wave of investment that is coming into” Malaysia, Haris added.

A large share of data centre investment flowing into Malaysia has been earmarked for Johor, which is adjacent to land-constrained Singapore. But as investment pledges roll in, Haris warned that energy constraints will need to be addressed for the region to realise its full potential.

See also: SoftBank’s Son plans US$50 bil Malaysian tech outlay, says Anwar

Data centres have signed agreements with Malaysia’s power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) for as much as 8.77 gigawatts of peak demand, according to officials, equivalent to almost a third of 2025 installed capacity. More power generation will be needed if the industry is to expand. In Johor, the centres could consume as much as 23% of Peninsular Malaysia’s energy supply by 2031, according to BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.

SD Guthrie has over 210,000 hectares (519,000 acres) of freehold land, making the company Malaysia’s largest landowner, and has earmarked roughly 10% of its current landbank for industrial development, along with renewable energy assets. The palm oil producer expects income from industrial development to account for a third of its revenue by the end of the decade, Haris said.

Even as it seeks to capitalise on the data centre boom, SD Guthrie’s core palm oil business faces a more uncertain supply outlook. Haris said Malaysian production is expected to remain steady at around 20 million tons next year despite a severe El Niño, although dry weather across Indonesia will likely disrupt crop development and delay fruit ripening. The company operates plantations in both countries.

See also: Debt repayment looms for Genting

“The concern is in Indonesia,” said Haris, adding that haze stemming from wildfires is slowing harvesting at estates in Kalimantan and Sumatra and could weigh on productivity. “Indonesia may potentially struggle with crop size next year and this could then become a supply problem for the industry.”

Malaysia, the world’s second-biggest grower, is currently grappling with a supply glut but Haris sees stockpiles starting to decline by February or March, helping to support prices. He expects benchmark palm oil futures to climb to around RM5,000 (US$1,224) a ton by the end of the first quarter of 2027 on slowing output and firm demand. They are currently near RM4,800 a ton.

SD Guthrie is keen to expand in Indonesia even as greater state control over the commodities sector creates some “uncertainty and angst” among producers, Haris said. The company’s operations haven’t been disrupted by the policy shifts, he added, which include plans for centralized export controls.

“I would be willing to double down on Indonesia, with the right assets to acquire and with the right partners,” Haris said. “It may not be in upstream, but I’m quite interested to look at downstream.”

title: Sembcorp and ST Engineering prepare for nuclear future
article:
Sembcorp Industries has announced that subsidiary Sembcorp Utilities has signed separate nonbinding memoranda of understanding with Canadian nuclear power engineering services AtkinsRéalis and fellow Mainboard-listed company ST Engineering.

Under the MoU with AtkinsRéalis, the companies will share knowledge and perspectives on nuclear energy technologies and industry developments, including technical, safety, regulatory, economic and commercial considerations. The companies will also explore collaboration opportunities in the nuclear energy sector.

Under the MoU with ST Engineering, the knowledge exchange will focus on nuclear technologies, supply chains and international industry practices, as well as training and talent development.

AtkinsRéalis is the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and exclusive license holder of Canadian CANDU (Canadian Deuterium Uranium) nuclear technology through its subsidiary Candu Energy. It has built a total of 34 CANDU conventional nuclear reactors worldwide. The company has designed a CANDU SMR utilising heavy-water and natural-uranium technology, but no full-scale unit is currently operational.

“These partnerships will enable the knowledge build-up and capability development for nuclear energy technologies,” says Sembcorp COO Charles Koh. “Alongside nearer-term solutions such as our upcoming hydrogen-ready power plant, we are supporting energy security and transition, while positioning our energy business for future opportunities”

ST Engineering, which has been building relevant capabilities and technologies in nuclear, including delivering specialised tungsten coatings for fusion reactor applications and initiating materials research, notes that developing expertise and capabilities in the nuclear industry takes time. “Through this collaboration with Sembcorp, we can deepen our understanding of the nuclear energy ecosystem, build on this technical expertise, and explore the deployment of ST Engineering’s deep capabilities in advanced engineering, mission-critical command and control systems and cybersecurity as the sector develops,” says Lee Shiang Long, group chief technology and digital officer at ST Engineering.

See also: Singapore shields itself from energy risks as Indonesia cuts gas

Joe St. Julian, president, nuclear, AtkinsRéalis, points out that nuclear energy is recognised as an “essential” part of a secure, reliable and low-carbon energy system. “As the original equipment manufacturer of CANDU technology, one of the world’s leading nuclear technologies, AtkinsRéalis brings more than six decades of nuclear expertise to this collaboration,” says St. Julian. “Through this agreement, AtkinsRéalis and Sembcorp will combine our respective experience and insights to support knowledge sharing and capabilities development in the nuclear sector.”

Singapore will undertake an Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review (INIR) Phase 1 Mission starting in 2027. The city-state is actively studying the feasibility of deploying SMRs as part of its long-term strategy to achieve energy security.
